name: Confirmation Bias
description: People seek, notice, and interpret evidence in ways that support what they already believe or expect. Once a hypothesis takes hold, contradictory evidence is easy to miss unless the process explicitly looks for it.
design_relevance_note: Critical in user research, analytics interpretation, A/B test readouts, heuristic reviews, and roadmap debates where teams can over-weight confirming signals and ignore disconfirming ones.
myth_risk_note: The behavioral phenomenon (people favor belief-supportive information) is robust and undisputed, but the standard framing -- an irrational motivation to confirm -- is disputed by Klayman & Ha's (1987) reinterpretation as a largely rational "positive test strategy" under realistic sparse-hypothesis conditions.
prevalence_note: Core concept in UX research, experimentation, and evidence-based product practice; routinely taught in research-methods and behavioral-design curricula.

findings.description: Across a wide range of contexts (hypothesis testing, everyday reasoning, group decision-making, self-perception, and more), people systematically seek and interpret evidence in ways that favor their existing beliefs or the hypothesis they're currently entertaining — a pervasive, well-evidenced tendency rather than a narrow laboratory artifact, though whether it serves any adaptive function or is purely a liability remains genuinely debated.
findings.source_title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises

findings.description: In an inductive rule-discovery task, only 6 of 29 subjects reached the correct conclusion without an incorrect one first; 22 of 29 reached at least one wrong conclusion, and those who reached two or more wrong conclusions were largely unwilling or unable to actually test their hypotheses by seeking disconfirming evidence — the founding experimental demonstration of confirmation bias in hypothesis-testing behavior.
findings.source_title: On the Failure to Eliminate Hypotheses in a Conceptual Task

applications.title: Danish politicians read the same performance data differently depending on political framing
applications.description: The UK's Behavioural Insights Team (BIT) describes a study in which 127 elected Danish politicians were shown hypothetical satisfaction statistics for two schools and asked to identify the better-performing one. When the options were labeled innocuously ('School A' and 'School B'), about 75% answered correctly. When the same options were instead framed as 'Public School' vs. 'Private School' -- a politically contentious framing in Denmark -- accuracy split sharply along prior belief: 92% answered correctly when the correct answer matched their existing views on public services, but only 56% did when it contradicted those views. Politicians given more information performed worse, relying more heavily on prior attitudes rather than the added data.
applications.ethical_note: A behavioral-science research finding about how political motivated reasoning distorts evidence interpretation among elected officials -- included as a real, quantified illustration of confirmation bias in a governance context, not a persuasion technique.

applications.title: Hypothetical: a leading survey question that confirms the designers' checkout-button hypothesis
applications.description: NN/g's own illustrative example: designers of an ecommerce site assume low sales are caused by a poorly designed checkout button, then write a leading survey question ('Was the red checkout button difficult to locate?') that primes respondents toward confirming that specific hypothesis instead of surfacing the real underlying problem with the checkout flow.
applications.ethical_note: This is a researcher-side methodology failure -- a leading question that biases internal decision-making -- not a technique aimed at persuading end users, so there is no user-facing persuasion/manipulation dimension to grade here, unlike anchoring or scarcity applications elsewhere in this corpus.

applications.title: Michael Aagaard's client redesign that overturned a 'people don't read online' assumption
applications.description: CRO practitioner Michael Aagaard (then Senior Conversion Optimizer at Unbounce) describes a real, anonymized client selling an expensive subscription product whose website assumed 'people don't read online' and kept product pages minimal. Customer surveys revealed unanswered questions about the subscription; new, much more information-dense product pages addressing those questions produced a stated five-figure revenue increase within the first 14 days of testing.
applications.ethical_note: The fix here was surfacing real information users were actively asking for (subscription mechanics, hidden fees) that the original minimal pages omitted -- a case of correcting an internal assumption to serve users better, not a persuasion technique aimed at extracting more from them. The vague 'five-figure' framing and anonymized client are graded honestly as unverifiable specifics rather than treated as a precise, confirmed number.
